name: Ngarla
confidence_why: 7 independent first-hand descriptions agree (1 state the same rule, 5 refine it); none contradicts.

new_statements.quote: Stress in Ngarla is predictable. [...] According to Geytenbeek (2006), the stress placement rules of Ngarla are as shown in Table 7. A few longer suffixes (-kujarra 'exclusively', 'completely'; -rukarra 'similar to'; -pungkara 'associated with specific location') however have their own main stress, which invariably falls on the second syllable (Geytenbeek 2006). [Table 7:] One to three syllable words: Main stress on 1st syllable, no secondary stress. Four syllable words: Main stress on 1st syllable, secondary stress on 3rd syllable. Five syllable words: Main stress on 1st syllable, secondary stress on 4th syllable. Six syllable words: Main stress on 1st syllable, secondary stress on 3rd and 5th syllables. [p.39:] main stress always falls on the first syllable of a word.

new_statements.locator: sec. 2.3 'Stress placement rules', p. 10 (p. 22), Table 7; phonological-word note p. 39 (p. 51)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: ): p.22 = printed p.10 carries heading '2.3 Stress placement rules'; the sentences 'Stress in Ngarla is predictable.', 'According to Geytenbeek (2006), the stress placement rules of Ngarla are as shown in Table 7. A few longer suffixes (-kujarra.. -rukarra.. -pungkara..) however have their own main stress, which invariably falls on the second syllable (Geytenbeek 2006).' and all four Table 7 rows (1-3 syll: main on 1st, no secondary; 4 syll: secondary on 3rd; 5 syll: secondary on 4th; 6 syll: secondary on 3rd and 5th) are there word for word; the compiler '[..]' correctly elides the Goedemans (1998:242, 244) sentences, which I also verified. Footnote 15 (kujarra 'two' vs suffix -kujarra) ve…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog stress placement coded per word length as 10 100 1010 10010 101010 (1 = a stressed syllable) (Table 7 is its exact source pattern); adds the suffix exceptions, the phonological-word domain (verbalisers stressed separately) and the Goedemans 1998 discrepancy.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable: main stress on the first syllable of every word regardless of length; secondary stress (per Geytenbeek 2006) on the 3rd syllable in 4-syllable words, the 4th in 5-syllable words, and the 3rd and 5th in 6-syllable words; none in words of 1-3 syllables. A few long suffixes carry their own main stress on their second syllable; most verbalisers attract main stress and so count as separate phonological words.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Table 7 (from Geytenbeek 2006): none in 1-3 syllable words; on the 3rd syllable in 4-syllable words; on the 4th in 5-syllable words; on the 3rd and 5th in 6-syllable words.
new_statements.exceptions: Long suffixes -kujarra 'exclusively/completely', -rukarra 'similar to', -pungkara 'associated with specific location' have their own main stress on their second syllable (distinguishing suffix -kujarra from the numeral kujarra 'two', which is initially stressed). Most verbalisers attract main stress on their first syllable and are phonological words in their own right; the -rri-Ø and -rni-L verbalisers do not (p. 39). Westerlund notes Goedemans (1998:242,244) listed Ngarla under 'initial stress with frequent stress on second, no regularities discovered', which he attributes to lack of data.
new_statements.identity_note: All statements are about Ngarla proper (Ngayarta, Pama-Nyungan), based on Geytenbeek's Ngarla-English dictionary material. The 2007 appendix is a pronunciation guide framed for the eastern-Pilbara phonemic alphabet in general but illustrated with Ngarla words; no dialect distinctions are made.

new_statements.quote: As a primary rule stress should be placed on the first syllable of each word (as in the English noun permit, "a licence"), not the second syllable (as in the verb permit, "allow"). In words of four or five syllables, the second-to-last syllable is also stressed, though more lightly than the first. A predictable exception occurs only in words of five or more phonemes, and only when sequences within such words begin with /k/, /p/, or /t/, are followed by /i/ or /u/, and then by /r/ or /w/. In such cases the first vowel is shortened or even omitted, and if there would have been stress on that vowel it is transferred onto the next vowel, which is then sometimes slightly lengthened.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: ): p.72 = printed p.72 is the 'Appendix: Pronunciation guidelines for the phonemic alphabet used for the Aboriginal languages of eastern Pilbara', 'adapted from Geytenbeek 2006a:6'. The quoted passage from 'As a primary rule stress should be placed on the first syllable of each word..' through '.. which is then sometimes slightly lengthened.' is there verbatim, followed by the kura-kura / kran-kran / pri:rri / kwa:rri / yuntri examples and 'The only other exceptions to the above rules are few and minor ones.' It is the only page in the thesis mentioning stress (a full-text search for stress/accent all 73 pages). Title page: 'A grammatical sketch of Ngarla: A language of Western Australia',…
new_statements.relation_note: Same initial main stress and same secondary positions for 4- and 5-syllable words as the catalog rule; adds the vowel-elision exception. Says nothing about 6-syllable words.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the first syllable of each word; in 4- and 5-syllable words the second-to-last syllable takes a lighter secondary stress. Predictable exception: in words of five or more phonemes, a /k, p, t/ + /i, u/ + /r, w/ sequence loses or shortens its vowel and any stress on it shifts to the next vowel (kuwarri 'now' > kwa:rri; pirirri > pri:rri).
new_statements.secondary_stress: In words of four or five syllables the second-to-last (penultimate) syllable is also stressed, more lightly than the first (= 3rd syllable of 4, 4th of 5; consistent with the catalog's 1010 and 10010).
new_statements.exceptions: Vowel reduction/elision in /k,p,t/ + /i,u/ + /r,w/ sequences in words of 5+ phonemes moves the stress to the following vowel (kuran-kuran > 'kran-kran', pirirri > 'pri:rri', kuwarri > 'kwa:rri', yunturi > 'yuntri'); 'the only other exceptions to the above rules are few and minor ones'. The guidelines are stated for the eastern-Pilbara phonemic alphabet generally (adapted from Geytenbeek 2006a:6), with Ngarla examples.
new_statements.identity_note: All statements are about Ngarla proper (Ngayarta, Pama-Nyungan), based on Geytenbeek's Ngarla-English dictionary material. The 2007 appendix is a pronunciation guide framed for the eastern-Pilbara phonemic alphabet in general but illustrated with Ngarla words; no dialect distinctions are made.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: Identity: Westerlund's Ngarla is the Ngayarta (Pilbara, Port Hedland) language = Glottolog ngar1296; no languoid confusion. Quote: confirmed verbatim at the stated place (sec. 2.3, Table 7, p.10) in the ANU open-access PDF, downloaded now because the record held no file. Coding: stress placement coded per word length as 10 100 1010 10010 101010 (1 = a stressed syllable) reproduces Table 7 exactly (initial main stress; secondary on the penult in 4-5 syllable words, 3rd+5th in 6-syllable words), so 'fixed-dominant, initial' stands. not in the strict set/in the dominant set is also right: the source itself lists lexical exceptions (three long suffixes carry their own main stress on their 2nd syllable) and the Geytenbeek pronunciation guide relayed in Westerlund 2007 p.72 adds a predictable phonetic exception (initial-vowel elision in /k p t/+/i u/+/r w/ sequences shifts stress to the next vowel, pirirri -> 'pri:rri'). Source quality: the deciding work is the only reference
